'''''Pittosporum tenuifolium''''' is a small [[evergreen]] tree endemic to [[New Zealand]] – growing up to {{convert|10|m|ft|0|abbr=on}} – commonly known as '''{{lang|mi|kōhūhū}}''' and '''black matipo''', and by other [[Māori people|Māori]] names '''{{lang|mi|kohukohu}}''' and '''{{lang|mi|tawhiwhi}}'''. Its small, very dark, reddish-purple flowers generally go unnoticed, and are scented only at night. The Latin {{lang|la|tenuifolium}} means "slender-leaved".<ref name="RHSLG">{{cite book|last=Harrison|first=Lorraine|title=RHS Latin for gardeners|year=2012|publisher=Mitchell Beazley|location=United Kingdom|isbn=9781845337315|pages=224}}</ref>

==Description==
''Pittosporum'' translates to tarry – {{Transliteration|la|pittos}} – seed – {{Transliteration|la|sporum}},<ref name=":3">{{Cite book|title=Native edible plants of New Zealand|last=Crowe, Andrew.|date=1990|publisher=Hodder and Stoughton|isbn=0340508302|oclc=768637129}}</ref> a reference to the sticky fluid that encases the seeds<ref name=":0" /> and {{lang|la|tenuifolium}} means thin – {{lang|la|tenui}} – leaf – {{lang|la|folium}}.<ref name=":3" />

{{lang|mi|Kōhūhū|italic=no}} is a bush or small tree that grows up to around 8–10 metres tall. The [[Trunk (botany)|trunk]] is slender (30–40 cm diameter) with a [[mottle]]d dark grey bark color<ref name=":0" /> that progressively turns black towards the tips of the branches.<ref name=":4">{{Cite book|title=New Zealand's native trees|last=Dawson |first= John |isbn=9781877517013|oclc=832592658|year = 2011|publisher=Craig Potton }}</ref>

The leaf coverage is compact in {{lang|mi|kōhūhū|italic=no}}; the leaves are arranged [[Alternate leaf|alternately]] on the [[Plant stem|stem]]<ref name=":0" /> and the [[Petiole (botany)|petiole]] is short.<ref name=":0" /> The leaves themselves are usually small – 2–4 cm long by 1–2 cm wide – but can grow up to 7 cm long.<ref name=":0" /> The edges are [[Glossary of leaf morphology#Edge|undulated]] and the leaf shape can range from oval to almost circular.<ref name=":4" /> Young leaves are covered in a layer of fine hairs that gets shed as the leaves grow.<ref name=":0" /> Adult leaves have a smooth, glossy texture.<ref name=":6">{{Cite book|title=Plant heritage New Zealand = te whakapapa o nga rakau : interpreting the special features of native plants|last=Foster |first= Tony |date= 2012 |orig-date=1957 |publisher=Bushmans Friend |isbn=9780473219123|oclc=840603084}}</ref> The colouration of the foliage is a silvery green,<ref name=":4" /> darker on the upper side and lighter underneath.<ref name=":6" /> The [[Glossary of botanical terms#midrib|midrib]] of the leaf and its smaller lateral veins are whiteish and quite visible on the upper side of the leaf.<ref name=":0" />

{{lang|mi|Kōhūhū|italic=no}} has small – around 1 cm in diameter – dark coloured flowers.<ref name=":4" /> The colour ranges from dark-red<ref name=":6" /> to dark-purple<ref name=":4" /> turning almost black as the flowers age.<ref name=":0" /> On rare occasions, the colour can be red or yellow.<ref name=":4" /> The flowers develop from [[Axillary bud|lateral buds]], either individually or in clumps,<ref name=":4" /> and can be male or [[Bisexual flower|bisexual]].<ref name=":4" />

The flowers are filled with nectar and exude a honey scented fragrance in the evenings with the scent being more obvious in slightly damp conditions.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Moore |first=Lucy B. |title=The Oxford book of New Zealand plants |last2=Irwin |first2=J. B. |date=1978 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0-19-558035-8 |location=Wellington; New York}}</ref> This attracts moths and night flying insects, and it is believed these insects help with pollination.<ref name=":0" />

Fertilised flowers develop into small – around 1.2 cm in diameter – <ref name=":0" /> globe shaped fruits.<ref name=":5">{{Cite book|title=Flora of New Zealand. Psilopsida, Lycopsida, Filicopsida, Gymnospermae, Dicotyledones|last=Allan | first = H. H. |date=1982|publisher=Government Printer|isbn=0477010563|oclc=760926043}}</ref> The fruit is covered in a small layer of hairs during early maturation that is progressively discarded as the capsule ripens.<ref name=":0" /> In the ripening process the [[Capsule (fruit)|capsule]] shrinks, hardens up and turns almost black, splitting into two or three segments when ripened.<ref name=":0" /> Inside are black seeds, encased in a very sticky substance.<ref name=":0" /> The stickiness of the seeds is likely to help with seed dispersal.

== Distribution ==

=== Natural global range ===
{{lang|mi|Kōhūhū|italic=no}} is endemic to New Zealand.<ref name=":0"/>

=== New Zealand range ===
{{lang|mi|Kōhūhū|italic=no}} is well spread all over New Zealand, being absent only to the west of the [[Southern Alps]]<ref name=":5" /> and [[Stewart Island]].<ref name=":0" />

=== Habitat preferences ===
{{lang|mi|Kōhūhū|italic=no}} is found growing wild in coastal and lower mountain forest areas up to an altitude of 900 m.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.rhs.org.uk/getattachment/cf6798ef-db1b-4be9-a2d0-32fbd76c5bfd/Pittosporum-tenuifolium-Plant-Assessment.aspx|title=Pittosporum tenuifolium hybrids and cultivars|last=Miller|first=Diana M.|publisher=Royal Horticultural Society|access-date=27 May 2013|archive-date=27 May 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130527212227/http://www.rhs.org.uk/getattachment/cf6798ef-db1b-4be9-a2d0-32fbd76c5bfd/Pittosporum-tenuifolium-Plant-Assessment.aspx|url-status=live}}</ref>

{{lang|mi|Kōhūhū|italic=no}} grows particularly quickly at forest edges<ref name=":4" /> located at the bottom of high [[Terrace (geology)|terraces]],<ref name=":0" /> and can also be found growing in [[Stream bed|riverbeds]].<ref name=":0" /> It grows readily in forested areas that have been disturbed<ref name=":4" /> or in reverting farmland, playing an important role in [[ecological succession]].<ref name=":0" />

==Life cycle/Phenology==
[[File:Pittosporum tenuifolium (Kohuhu) capsule.jpg|thumb|The capsule of {{lang|mi|kōhūhū|italic=no}}, showing the black seeds encased in a sticky substance]]
Most of the plants in the genus ''Pittosporum'' are easily propagated from seed, but germination may be slow.<ref name=":0" /> In horticultural production, the sticky substance coating the seeds is removed before sowing, as it acts as a germination inhibitor. The seeds are treated to simulate natural conditions for six weeks in order to improve germination rates.<ref name=":0" />

{{lang|mi|Kōhūhū|italic=no}} is a relatively fast growing plant<ref name=":0" /> growing from 0.5 metres to 3 metres within five years. The root system is shallow and spread out.<ref name=":7">{{Cite web|url=https://icm.landcareresearch.co.nz/research/freshwater/documents/Kohuhu.pdf|title=Kohuhu Pittosporum tenuifolium|website=Landcare Research|access-date=2024-12-22|archive-date=2023-01-30|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230130012739/https://icm.landcareresearch.co.nz/research/freshwater/documents/Kohuhu.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref> These characteristics make it ideal – when used in conjunction with another plants – for use in stream stabilisation<ref name=":7" /> and [[erosion control]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Marden|first1=M.|last2=Lambie|first2=S.|last3=Rowan|first3=D.|date=2018-07-11|title=Root system attributes of 12 juvenile indigenous early colonising shrub and tree species with potential for mitigating erosion in New Zealand |journal=New Zealand Journal of Forestry Science |volume=48 |issue=1 |doi=10.1186/s40490-018-0115-9 |issn=1179-5395 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

Flowering happens in late spring, from October to November, and the maturation of the fruit happens between mid-summer and autumn, from January to March.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.nzflora.info/factsheet/Taxon/Pittosporum-tenuifolium.html|title=Flora of New Zealand {{!}} Taxon Profile {{!}} Pittosporum tenuifolium|website=www.nzflora.info|access-date=2019-05-13}}</ref>

The seedlings of {{lang|mi|kōhūhū|italic=no}} are unusual, as in some cases they have three or four [[Cotyledon|seed leaves]] instead of the usual two.<ref name=":6"/>
[[File:Pittosporum tenuifolium tree.jpg|180px|thumb|right|Medium-sized {{lang|mi|kōhūhū|italic=no}} tree in Queenstown, New Zealand]]

==Diet and foraging==
{{lang|mi|Kōhūhū|italic=no}} is a hardy plant that can cope with poor conditions – poor soils, droughts and windy environments.<ref name=":0" /> It is, however, a light-demanding plant<ref name=":0" /> and prefers soils with good drainage in humid climates.<ref name=":8">{{Cite book|title=The gardener's encyclopaedia of New Zealand native plants|last=Cave, Yvonne.|date=1999|publisher=Random House|others=Paddison, Valda.|isbn=1869620437|location=Auckland|oclc=44289301}}</ref> Planting it in damp conditions can cause winter leaf drop,<ref name=":8" /> which likely explains why {{lang|mi|kōhūhū|italic=no}} is not found growing on the [[West Coast, New Zealand|West Coast]] of New Zealand. In its role in [[ecological succession]], {{lang|mi|kōhūhū|italic=no}} is often found at an earlier stage than its relative [[Pittosporum eugenioides|lemonwood]] (another endemic ''Pittosporum''), and usually inhabits less fertile soils.<ref name=":0" />

==Predators, Parasites, and Diseases==

=== Insects ===
[[File:Pittosporum tenuifolium kz5.jpg|thumb|The small, dark flower of {{lang|mi|kōhūhū|italic=no}}]]
There are over 50 insect species listed in the Plant-SyNZ database<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://plant-synz.landcareresearch.co.nz/ReportForm.aspx?RecordId=274&Type=P&ReportType=Adv&SortBy=Alpha&Biostatus=a|title=PlantSynz - Invertebrate herbivore biodiversity assessment tool: Database|website=Plant-SyNZ|access-date=2019-05-05|archive-date=2021-06-04|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210604124304/https://plant-synz.landcareresearch.co.nz/ReportForm.aspx?RecordId=274&Type=P&ReportType=Adv&SortBy=Alpha&Biostatus=a|url-status=live}}</ref> that either feed on or [[Parasitism|parasitise]] {{lang|mi|kōhūhū|italic=no}}, including wasps, sucking bugs, flies, [[moth]]s, butterflies, [[Thrips (genus)|thrips]], [[mite]]s and [[beetle]]s. There are also more than a dozen beetles that feed on the dead plant material.

Below are some species of interest, organised by feeding habits:

Pittosporum flower weevil (''[[Aneuma rubricale]]''), a native insect, lays its eggs on the flower of {{lang|mi|kōhūhū|italic=no}}; interestingly, only {{lang|mi|kōhūhū|italic=no}} is chosen for this, even if the weevil feeds on other types of ''Pittosporum''. As soon as the weevil's larvae hatch, they start feeding on the [[stamen]]s and [[Ovary (botany)|ovaries]] of the flowers, switching to the leaves once they reach adulthood.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://nzacfactsheets.landcareresearch.co.nz/factsheet/InterestingInsects/Pittosporum-flower-weevil---Aneuma-rubricale.html|title=Pittosporum flower weevil - ''Aneuma rubricale''|last=Martin|first=N. A.|date=2018|website=Interesting Insects and other Invertebrates|access-date=2024-12-22|archive-date=2023-11-19|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231119005057/https://nzacfactsheets.landcareresearch.co.nz/factsheet/InterestingInsects/Pittosporum-flower-weevil---Aneuma-rubricale.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

An arrival from Australia, pittosporum shield bug (''Monteithiella humeralis'')<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://nzacfactsheets.landcareresearch.co.nz/factsheet/InterestingInsects/Pittosporum-shield-bug---Monteithiella-humeralis.html|title=Factsheet: Pittosporum shield bug - Monteithiella humeralis|last=Martin|first=N. A.|date=2018|website=Interesting Insects & other Invertebrates|access-date=2019-05-05|archive-date=2019-01-24|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190124130915/https://nzacfactsheets.landcareresearch.co.nz/factsheet/InterestingInsects/Pittosporum-shield-bug---Monteithiella-humeralis.html|url-status=live}}</ref> as well as the endemic pittosporum [[Psyllidae|psyllid]] ''Trioza vitreoradiata''<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://nzacfactsheets.landcareresearch.co.nz/factsheet/InterestingInsects/Pittosporum-psyllid---Trioza-vitreoradiata.html|title=Factsheet: Pittosporum psyllid - ''Trioza vitreoradiata''|last=Martin|first=N. A.|date=2018|website=Interesting Insects & other Invertebrates|access-date=2019-05-05|archive-date=2019-01-24|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190124121830/https://nzacfactsheets.landcareresearch.co.nz/factsheet/InterestingInsects/Pittosporum-psyllid---Trioza-vitreoradiata.html|url-status=live}}</ref> feed only on ''Pittosporum'' species, by attaching themselves to a suitable part of the plant and feeding on its [[sap]]. The [[Psyllidae|psyllid]] leaves a trail of characteristic "beads" behind.

Cottony cushion scale (''[[Icerya purchasi]]''),<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://nzacfactsheets.landcareresearch.co.nz/factsheet/InterestingInsects/Cottony-cushion-scale---Icerya-purchasi.html|title=Factsheet: Cottony cushion scale - ''Icerya purchasi''|last=Martin|first=N. A.|date=2018|website=Interesting Insects & other Invertebrates|access-date=2019-05-05|archive-date=2019-01-23|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190123101551/https://nzacfactsheets.landcareresearch.co.nz/factsheet/InterestingInsects/Cottony-cushion-scale---Icerya-purchasi.html|url-status=live}}</ref> an Australian bug, soft wax scale (''[[Ceroplastes destructor]]''), an import from overseas<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://nzacfactsheets.landcareresearch.co.nz/factsheet/InterestingInsects/Soft-wax-scale---Ceroplastes-destructor.html|title=Factsheet: Soft wax scale - ''Ceroplastes destructor''|last=Martin|first=N. All attach themselves to a suitable part of the plant and feed on its sap.

New Zealand flower thrips (''[[Thrips obscuratus]]'') feeds on leaves, flowers and young fruit of {{lang|mi|kōhūhū|italic=no}}, by piercing plant cells and sucking their contents.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://nzacfactsheets.landcareresearch.co.nz/factsheet/InterestingInsects/New-Zealand-flower-thrips---Thrips-obscuratus.html|title=Factsheet: New Zealand flower thrips - ''Thrips obscuratus''|last=Martin|first=N. A.|date=2019|website=Interesting Insects & other Invertebrates|access-date=2019-05-05|archive-date=2019-01-24|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190124102830/https://nzacfactsheets.landcareresearch.co.nz/factsheet/InterestingInsects/New-Zealand-flower-thrips---Thrips-obscuratus.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

=== Fungi ===
''[[Pythium irregulare]]'' has been recorded as a [[pathogen]] of {{lang|mi|kōhūhū|italic=no}}, causing foliar [[blight]], rot, and eventually death.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Guarnaccia |first1=Vladimiro |last2=Hansen |first2=Zachariah R. |last3=Aiello |first3=Dalia |last4=Smart |first4=Christine D. |last5=Polizzi |first5=Giancarlo |date=2015 |title=First Detection of Root Rot and Foliar Blight on ''Pittosporum'' (''Pittosporum tenuifolium'') Caused by ''Pythium irregulare'' in Italy |journal=Journal of Phytopathology |language=en|volume=163|issue=5|pages=411–414|doi=10.1111/jph.12290|issn=1439-0434|doi-access=free }}</ref>

A recently discovered pathogen of {{lang|mi|kōhūhū|italic=no}} that caused swelling of twigs, the fungus ''[[Elsinoe takoropuku]]'', turned out to be a newly discovered species of fungi. The fungus was, so far, only found in association with {{lang|mi|kōhūhū|italic=no}}.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Ridley|first1=G. S.|last2=Ramsfield|first2=T. D.|date=2005-11-01 |title=''Elsinoe takoropuku'' sp. nov. infects twigs of ''Pittosporum tenuifolium'' in New Zealand |journal=Mycologia |volume=97 |issue=6 |pages=1362–1364 |doi=10.1080/15572536.2006.11832742 |pmid=16722226 |s2cid=218589359|issn=0027-5514}}</ref>

==Uses==
=== Garden plant ===
{{lang|mi|Kōhūhū|italic=no}} is a popular garden plant in New Zealand and overseas, often used a hedge or as visual backdrop.<ref name=":0" /> It is sometimes grown under the cultivar name 'Nigricans', so called because of its black stems. In horticulture it is valued for its coloured foliage (cultivated variations include purple, "silver" and variegated leaves), and for its tolerance of some horticulturally difficult growing conditions, including dry soils and shade (although in northwest Europe, cold and exposed situations do not suit it).

Several [[Hybrid (biology)#Hybrid plants|hybrid]]s and [[cultivar]]s have been developed<ref name=":0" /> and five varieties won the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]] due to their ability to cope in the growing conditions of the United Kingdom:<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf|title=AGM Plants - Ornamental|date=July 2017|publisher=Royal Horticultural Society|page=79|access-date=2 May 2018|archive-date=5 January 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180105180412/https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref>

=== Host of threatened wood rose ===
[[File:Wood roses in the Whanganui Regional Museum collection.jpg|thumb|The structure formed by the threatened root parasite wood rose]]
{{lang|mi|Kōhūhū|italic=no}} has the potential to be used as the host of the threatened root parasite plant wood rose (''[[Dactylanthus taylorii]]''). Wood rose was recently successfully [[Species translocation|translocated]] and sown in the wild from seed, showing the largest success rate when planted in association with kōhūhū.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Holzapfel|first1=Sebastian Avi|last2=Dodgson |first2=John |last3=Rohan |first3=Maheshwaran |date=2016-02-01 |title=Successful translocation of the threatened New Zealand root-holoparasite ''Dactylanthus taylorii'' (Mystropetalaceae) |journal=Plant Ecology |language=en |volume=217 |issue=2 |pages=127–138 |doi=10.1007/s11258-015-0556-7|issn=1573-5052|doi-access=free}}</ref>

=== Use by Māori ===
There are several recorded uses of {{lang|mi|kōhūhū|italic=no}} by [[Māori people|Māori]]. The resin and oils extracted from the leaves have been used for their scent and often mixed with ingredients sourced from other native trees in order to produce an oil of variable composition.<ref name=":1">{{Cite book|title=Māori Healing and Herbal|last=Riley|first=M.|publisher=Viking Sevenseas N.Z. Ltd|year=1997|location=Paraparaumu, New Zealand}}</ref> The resin is obtained by making cuts in the bark of the tree<ref name=":0" /> and the leaves crushed and mixed with other oils.<ref name=":1" /> The oil is used to scent little pouches<ref name=":0" /> or a dead bird skin,<ref name=":1" /> often worn around the neck.<ref name=":0" /> The oil is also used to scent houses and mats of people of high rank.<ref name=":1" />

In addition, {{lang|mi|kōhūhū|italic=no}} has been used for medicinal purposes by Māori. The resin has been mixed with other gums and chewed as a cure for bad breath and sores in the mouth.<ref name=":2">{{Cite book|title=Māori Healing Remedies |last=Riley |first=M. |publisher=Viking Sevenseas N.Z. Ltd |year=2018|location=Paraparaumu, New Zealand}}</ref> Parts of the plants have been used as [[Topical medication|topical treatment]] for relief of the symptoms of skin diseases.<ref name=":0" /> Crushed leaves  also have been used as a [[poultice]] for [[Ulcer (dermatology)|ulcers]].<ref>{{Cite book|title=New Zealand Medicinal Plants | first1 = S.G. | last1 = Brooker | first2 = R.C. | last2 = Cambie | first3 = R.C. | last3 = Cooper |publisher=Heinemann |year=1987 |location=Auckland, New Zealand}}</ref> The crushed bark has been soaked in water and the resulting mixture used to treat breast or chest ailments, and the remaining liquid taken orally.<ref name=":2" /> It has been used, together with [[Phormium|flax]] root, to make a brew used to treat fever, bleeding and [[Bruise|bruising]].<ref name=":2" /> Validating its traditional uses as a medicine, a 2010 study indicated that {{lang|mi|kōhūhū|italic=no}} does indeed possess some [[antimicrobial]] properties.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Earl|first1=Emma A.|last2=Altaf|first2=Mudassar|last3=Murikoli|first3=Rekha V.|last4=Swift|first4=Simon|last5=O'Toole|first5=Ronan|date=2010-06-10 |title=Native New Zealand plants with inhibitory activity towards Mycobacterium tuberculosis |journal=BMC Complementary and Alternative Medicine|volume=10|issue=1|pages=25|doi=10.1186/1472-6882-10-25|issn=1472-6882|pmc=2891623|pmid=20537175 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

The branches of {{lang|mi|kōhūhū|italic=no}} have been used in Māori life ceremonies, such as [[baptism]]s, and for welcoming visitors to a [[marae]]. Two of its common names, {{lang|mi|tāwhiri}} ("to wave to") and {{lang|mi|rautāwhiri}} ("to wave a leaf") reflect this.<ref name=":1" />
